shows.title: What Still Holds
shows.description:
Shilpa Gupta has built a three-decade career out of making the intangible — censorship, borders, surveillance, the fragility of memory — physically felt, and this survey-scale presentation inside the Kleihues Halle is her biggest German museum outing yet. The anchor is TRUTH, a room-filling sculpture of oversized freestanding letters that visitors have to walk between and around, turning an abstract word into an obstacle course. It's a blunt, almost comic gesture that becomes unsettling the longer you sit with it: what does it mean to physically navigate the idea of truth in a building that has itself served, at different points in history, very different political purposes?

Around that centerpiece, the show gathers pieces spanning Gupta's career-long interest in language as a site of control and resistance — hand-drawn maps redrawn from memory, a library of books published anonymously or under pseudonyms, sound and text works that toy with what can and can't be said aloud. Mumbai-born and based, Gupta has shown at the Barbican, MAXXI, and Centro Botín, and won the 2025 Possehl Prize for International Art; this is the kind of mid-career museum show that clarifies why she keeps getting invited back.

What makes the presentation especially sharp is its staging: it runs in deliberate dialogue with Hamburger Bahnhof's permanent Joseph Beuys collection display next door, the fourth time the museum has paired a woman artist against that canonical room. Beuys treated language and social sculpture as inseparable; Gupta, working from a very different political vantage point, asks similar questions about who gets to speak and be believed. Seeing the two shows back to back, as the museum clearly intends, is the most interesting way to spend an afternoon at Hamburger Bahnhof's 30th-anniversary program this year.

shows.title: This Time Tomorrow
shows.description:
Jordy Kerwick is a genuinely unlikely art-world success story — a self-taught, Melbourne-born painter who only picked up a brush in 2016 and has since built a body of work that trades in a loose, folkloric menagerie of animals, masks, and domestic clutter rendered in candy-bright oil and acrylic. This is his first Berlin solo show with König Galerie, staged in the atmospheric, half-buried Vault beneath St. Agnes, the gallery's brutalist former-church home in Kreuzberg.

The title borrows from The Kinks' 1970 song of the same name, and that lyric's shrug toward an uncertain future runs through the paintings on view. Kerwick works from small, specific details — a burst of magenta, the glint of water, a half-remembered domestic scene — and lets them accumulate into denser, stranger tableaux where the everyday tips into myth. Stripes, dots, and repeated marks give the surfaces a nervous, handmade energy; recurring hybrid creatures and masks turn straightforward still lifes into something closer to fable.

It's an unpretentious, colour-forward show, and a good example of König's willingness to mix outsider-adjacent, market-driven painters like Kerwick alongside its more conceptually rigorous program. Worth seeing in tandem with the building itself: the Vault's raw concrete and low light do a lot of work in making Kerwick's saturated palette feel almost theatrical.

shows.title: Kyiv Biennial: A Bird That Cannot Land
shows.description:
The Kyiv Biennial has never had a fixed home — since Russia's full-scale invasion forced it into exile, it has popped up in Warsaw, Antwerp, Dnipro, and Linz, among other cities — and this chapter turns KW's entire four-floor building over to its latest edition. More than 40 artists are packed into the show, ranging from internationally established names like Hito Steyerl, Mona Hatoum, and the late Geta Brătescu to younger Ukrainian, Central Asian, and Middle Eastern artists working in video, sound, sculpture, and performance.

The organizing idea is a loose geography the curators call "Middle-East-Europe," linking the post-Soviet East with Central and Southwest Asia and the Mediterranean — regions bound less by proximity than by shared histories of empire, displacement, and contested borders. Expect a lot of moving-image work and quietly devastating documentary material alongside more oblique, poetic pieces; the show leans hard into testimony and exile as subject matter without becoming a straightforward war-reportage exhibition.

Given Berlin's own large Ukrainian and Eastern European diaspora communities, staging this here rather than in a more neutral biennial city feels pointed, and KW has built out an unusually heavy parallel program of talks, screenings, and live performance alongside the galleries. It's a dense, demanding show — worth budgeting real time for — and one of the more substantial political-art statements in Berlin this year.
